steps: Site + uncrate
Allow for approx. 500lbs plus venting; a combustible floor or a raised base is fine. Lift off the wood top and supports, then remove the 4 pallet screws.

Leave room in front for the ember protection and clearances, and plan a chimney route that avoids cutting floor or roof joists. Where possible the chimney should penetrate the highest part of the roof, stay clear of roof offsets, trees and other obstructions, and use the fewest offsets.

  • Don't connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance.
  • Not inside a factory-built fireplace unless tested with it.
  • Manufactured or mobile home: not in a sleeping room. US installs follow HUD; in Canada, provide access openings whose covers need a household tool to open.
Frame the chase
Frame to the minimum dimensions in Fig. 6-7, allowing for drywall thickness, with 84" min from the unit base to the ceiling. No wood framing directly in front of the chimney system.
Set the unit + framing kit

Assemble the steel framing kit, push the fireplace in with the casing flush to the front framing (secure it if code requires), then set the kit on top legs-down, flush at the front, and fasten it to the chase framing.
Chimney

Listed 6" UL 103HT / ULC S629 chimney on the maker's anchor plate: 2" to combustibles, a firestop at every floor, three #8 x ½" stainless screws per joint. Outlet min 15' above the unit base, max 35'.

1. Plumb from the flue collar; cut and frame square holes; mount the firestops and radiation shields.
  2. Keep 2" to combustibles and don't fill the space with insulation; fit insulation shields as code requires.
  3. Insert the anchor plate into the flue collar, seal with stove cement and secure with stainless steel screws (spacer #11220002 for brands such as ICC).
  4. Assemble sections to rest on the anchor plate and protrude through the roof; avoid joints between the ceiling and the roof.
  5. Fit the roof radiation shield, flashing and storm collar, keeping the vapour barrier sealed.
  6. Roof braces if more than 5' above the roof; attach the rain cap and check the flashing for leaks.

Offsets: max four 30° elbows in the US (four 45° in Canada), supported per the chimney maker.
Combustion air

Outside air: 4" rigid or flex from the adapter (factory right side, swappable to the left) to an approved 4" inlet vent cap with rodent screen, at least 5 ft below the chimney outlet. Or use room air.
Blower wiring

Romex 14/2 through the strain relief into the junction box on the right side of the support base, to a wall switch or fan speed controller (not supplied). 115 V, 60 Hz, 1.1A, by a licensed electrician.
Ember protection + safety strip

2" metal safety strip the width of the unit, half under the front, with the gap sealed (e.g. sand-cement grout). Non-combustible ember protection: US 16 1/2" deep x 35" wide, Canada 18" x 57 1/2", 8" past each side of the door opening.
Remote heat kit (optional)
Kit #11490003, one or two per fireplace, on 6" listed B-vent, max 20 ft effective length each. Each kit needs a 30in² room air inlet in the chase.

1. Remove the top knockout panel for each kit and cut away the insulation below it.
  2. Fit the backflow damper (flap free, normally closed with the blower off), then the duct adapter over it with 4 screws.
  3. Mount the blower assembly so the casing/outlet grill is at least 12" from the ceiling or walls and 36" from the floor.
  4. Attach the 10" x 3 1/4" transition boot; run 6" Type B vent to the fireplace, screwed and sealed with aluminium foil tape.
  5. Wire it (120V, 60HZ, 80 watts), locate the chase make-up air inlet, keep drywall off the blower opening, refit the face plate and fit the grills.

Inlets for two kits can be combined if 60in² or greater. Without a kit no chase air inlet is required, though a single inlet and outlet is recommended.

The kit appears under two numbers: the rating label lists the optional remote heat kit as PART# WODC.RHKA (p. 3), and the kit's installation instructions give Part # 11490003 for the Remote Heat Transfer Kit (p. 24).
Finish the chase + trim

Cement board over the front facing from the floor to 7 ft above the unit bottom, 58" wide and centered, with nothing inside the facing edge/stop. Fit the backing plate (four screws) and hook on the front trim.

Only non-combustible finish within 11 1/2" of the outer edge of the door, under the door down to the floor, and up to at least 16" above the heat exchanger air deflector. Mantel (max 12" deep): 16" above the deflector. Side facing (max 4" deep): 11 1/2" from the door. Adjacent wall: 22" from the side of the door.

Front trim: line up its hooks with the locking slots in the brackets on either side of the firebox, push it in, then slide it down.
Firebricks
18 full-size and 5 cut bricks: rear 4 full-size plus one "C"; each side 4 full-size plus one "B"; floor 6 full-size plus "C" and "D".

A9" x 4 1/2" x 1 1/4" · 5096.99
B4 1/2" x 4 1/2" x 1 1/4" · 7847
C2 1/4" x 9" x 1 1/4" · 7847.3
D2 1/4" x 4 1/2" x 1 1/4" · 7847.1

The rear full-size bricks go two on each side of the baffle tube, with "C" in the back left corner. The floor pattern is shown as a drawing (Fig. 34).

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Never use chemicals or any other volatile liquid to start a fire. Don't leave the fireplace unattended while the door is open.

  1. Move the air control to High, all the way to the left.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the centre of the firebox and crisscross several pieces of small, dry kindling over it. Light the paper and leave the door ajar about 1" to 4" until the kindling is fully burning.
  3. When the kindling has burned down by half, add 2-3 small splits or small logs about 1" in diameter. Keep the door cracked open about 1" to 2" until they are fully lit.
  4. When that start-up wood has burned down by half and you have a good bed of coals, add your regular wood. Once it has caught, close the door and carry on with normal operation.
Slow to catch? Crack the door open 1" to 2" and close it as soon as the wood lights. Repeat if the flames start to die out.

Burn the wood right on the firebricks. Don't use a grate or andirons to raise it.

firstfire.title: Your first fires
firstfire.html:
The paint on your fireplace has to cure at operating temperature. That happens during your first 2-3 fires, and it gives off smoke and fumes while it does.

  • Open all the windows and doors so the room is well ventilated.
  • The curing smoke displaces oxygen. Small children, elderly people and anyone with breathing problems should leave the area during the hot burn. The smoke is mostly carbon dioxide: not toxic, but uncomfortable.
  • Follow the Stove Bright (Forrest Paint) information sheet that came with your fireplace.

Smoke alarm going off?

Smoke detectors may sound often while the paint cures, or if the door is accidentally left open. Don't disconnect them.

Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors may be required in the area where the fireplace is installed. Even where they aren't required, Pacific Energy strongly recommends them.

reload.title: Air control, reloading & overnight burns
reload.html:
The air control sets how hard the fire burns. High is all the way to the left. The minimum burn rate is set at the factory and must not be altered; federal regulations prohibit it.

Find your setting

Every home is different, so find your setting by trial and error and note it for next time. If smoke pours down across the glass (a "waterfall"), you turned the air down too soon or too low.

Reloading

  1. Move the air control to High and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly. This prevents backpuffing or flames rolling out.
  3. Load dry wood of different shapes and sizes so air can flow between the logs. Don't load higher than 7 1/2" above the firebox floor.

Overnight burns

Unsplit logs work best. Char the wood completely on High before you turn the air control to Low.

To restart, rake the hot embers toward the front, add a couple of dry split logs and close the door. Set the air to High; once the wood has charred, reset it.

Use High only for starting or preheating fresh loads. Long periods on High can over-fire the fireplace.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood gives higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwood or green, freshly cut wood.

  • Season wood for six months or more. Store it under cover, away from open flame or heat.
  • Wet or green wood smoulders, makes lots of smoke and creosote, gives little heat and tends to go out.

Test a piece

Put a large piece on a good bed of hot coals. Burning on more than one side within one minute: dry. Turns black and lights within three minutes: damp. Sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes: soaked, so don't burn it.

Never burn

Garbage, salt-water or treated wood, coal or charcoal, plywood, particleboard, cardboard or other paper products, lawn clippings or yard waste, railroad ties, construction or demolition debris, anything containing plastic, rubber (including tires) or asbestos, solvents, paints or paint thinners, waste petroleum or asphalt products, or manure or animal remains. Garbage and salt-water wood contain chlorides that destroy metal and void the warranty. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Note: p. 3 gives 16" as the ideal log length and 17" as the maximum; p. 7 recommends 17" logs.
Maker's website: Log Size (recommended) 16", Log Size (max) 18".

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Clean the glass only when the fireplace is cold, using fireplace glass cleaner. Don't use abrasive cleaners, and never scrape it with anything that might scratch.

What the deposit tells you

The deposit on the glass is a good sign of what is building up in your flue pipe and chimney.

  • Light brown and dusty, wipes off easily: good combustion and dry, well-seasoned wood, so the chimney is relatively clean.
  • Black and greasy, hard to remove: wet or green wood and too slow a burn. The same heavy deposit is building up just as quickly in the chimney.

If the glass keeps getting dirty, the usual causes are wet wood, turning the air down too soon, low draft, or a leaking door gasket.

Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the fireplace again. Use only the 5 mm ceramic glass your dealer supplies. Don't slam the door, and make sure no logs stick out where they could hit the glass.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Remove ashes only when the fire has burned down and both the ashes and the fireplace are cold.

  • Keep an ash base of 1" to 4". When the ashes get 3 to 4 inches deep, take out the excess.
  • Leave about 1" of ash on the firebox floor. It helps keep a hot charcoal bed for future fires.
  • Keep the front of the firebox clear. Boost combustion air enters there, and built-up ash blocks it.
  • Remove ashes often. Embers can roll out the door and start a fire.

Disposing of ashes

Put ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn. If you will bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have thoroughly cooled. Don't put other waste in the same container.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
A slow fire gives off tar and vapours that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it burns extremely hot. Some creosote is inevitable; regular inspection and cleaning is the answer.

  • Inspect and clean the chimney before your first fire of the season and at least every two months while you are burning.
  • Check daily for creosote buildup until experience shows you how often you need to clean to be safe.
  • Remove creosote once it builds up to 3 mm or more.
  • Burn dry wood with ample air: small loads (two or three logs, or 1/4 to 1/2 of a full load), with the air fairly wide open for the first 10 to 30 minutes after loading.
  • Have the chimney inspected by a certified professional (the manual names NFI, CSIA, WETT and APC).

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating.

If you have a chimney fire: get everyone ready to evacuate to your outside meeting place, close the air inlet and call the fire department. Keep a fire extinguisher handy. Before the next fire, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks, and check the combustibles around the chimney and the roof.

care.title: Routine checks, gasket, baffle & blowers
care.html:
Check these parts for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections or bad warping:

WeeklyFirebricks · door gasket
MonthlyBrick rails and tabs · air riser tube · back of the airwash chamber · baffle locking pin
When the chimney is cleanedBaffle and its board/blanket · baffle gasket · top heat shield and bolt · brick rails · manifold

Door gasket

The door seals with a 3/4" fibreglass rope gasket that needs only light pressure. Keep it in good condition and replace it when needed.

Baffle

Some warping is normal, up to 1/4". If it is warped more than that, cracked or broken, contact your dealer. Never run the fireplace with the baffle or its insulation removed.

Blowers

Clean the blowers at least once a year. Lift the front trim up and pull it away; there is a blower on each side of the firebox. Gently vacuum the dust from the intakes and the blower wheel.

Replace broken or missing firebricks. Running the fireplace with broken parts can damage other parts and may void your warranty.

safety.title: Safety & warning signs
safety.html:
• The fireplace is hot while it runs. Keep children, clothing and furniture away. Hot glass causes burns: don't touch it until it has cooled, and never let children touch it.
  • Keep the door closed while burning and open it only to add wood. An open door can draw too much air from the room and possibly cause suffocation.
  • Keep combustible materials 48" away. Don't store wood within the installation clearances, including in front of the fireplace.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids, and never barbecue in it.
  • Don't alter the air control. Tampering voids the warranty and can be very hazardous.

Over-firing

Do not over-fire the fireplace. Pushing for more heat than it is designed for can permanently damage it and the chimney. Causes include running with the door open, damaged door gaskets, burning kiln-dried lumber, mill ends or paper waste, and long or continual use on High.

Draft warning signs

A fire you can't control, or a part of the fireplace or chimney glowing red, means too much draft. Smoke leaking into the room through joints, or backpuffing, means too little.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy's warranty covers the original registered purchaser.

LTD lifetime coverage (10 years)Parts only: porcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage, not impact), plating, firebox and baffle
3 year comprehensiveParts and labor for any defective part, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches

Not covered

  • Labor under the lifetime coverage
  • Firebox rails and heat shields (not part of the lifetime coverage)
  • Firebrick, gaskets and ceramic fiber blankets
  • Parts showing misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance or modification

Premature wear usually points to improper use, such as excessive draft, heating too large an area, or contaminated fuel, and may void the warranty.

Making a claim

Report the problem to your Pacific Energy dealer with proof of purchase, the purchase date, and the model name and serial number. Register online at pacificenergy.net/register.

This is a summary. The full terms and exclusions are in the manual.

specChimney.title: Chimney
specChimney.html:
ChimneyListed 6" · UL 103HT (US) / CAN-ULC S629 (Canada)
Minimum height15' from the base of the unit to the chimney outlet

Above the roofRoof braces if more than 5' above the roof
OffsetsMax four 30° elbows (US) · four 45° elbows (Canada)

Use the chimney maker's fireplace anchor plate; some brands, including ICC, don't sit flush and need anchor plate spacer #11220002. Seal the anchor plate joint with stove cement and secure it with stainless steel screws. Use a radiation shield/firestop at every floor or wall the chimney passes through, and avoid joints between the ceiling and the roof. Offsets need a minimum 36" length of chimney before the first elbow. Don't connect to a flue serving another appliance.

Masonry chimney: fully lined with a liner listed to ULC S635, ULC S640 or UL1777, with ULC S629 or UL 103HT listed chimney for all parts inside the chase. It must serve this fireplace only and meet local codes or NFPA 211.

Note: p. 15 gives 35' (10.7m) as the recommended maximum chimney height (at sea level), measured from the top of the fireplace to the rain cap; p. 18 gives 35' as the maximum height of the chimney outlet, measured from the base of the unit.

Ember protection is non-combustible (tile, brick, slate, stone or metal) with a minimum K value of 23.7 btu/ft h °F, equivalent to 20GA steel. Half of the safety strip goes under the fireplace front and half extends under the hearth extension; seal the space between the fireplace and the hearth extension with a non-combustible material such as sand-cement grout. On a raised unit, a 2" x 2" angled piece can be used against the non-combustible face.

specFrame.html:

The unit may sit directly on a combustible floor or on a raised base. The minimum framing and enclosure dimensions are shown as drawings on this page (Fig. 6 and 7); adjust them for drywall, which counts as combustible. Install the top front framing as in Fig. 7, with no wood framing directly in front of the chimney system.

  • No insulation or loose fill in contact with the fireplace; cover chase insulation with drywall or non-combustible panels.
  • Don't insulate the front portion of the chase above the unit.
  • No recesses, shelves or cupboards above the fireplace, and nothing built inside the minimum chase area.
  • Manufactured or mobile homes: not in a sleeping room.

specAir.title: Combustion air
specAir.html:
Outside air duct4" rigid or flex (insulated flex recommended in cold climates)
AdapterFactory-installed on the right side; swaps with the left cover plate
Inlet capApproved 4" inlet vent cap, 20GA min. wire mesh rodent screen
Inlet locationAt least 5 ft below the chimney outlet

Outside air can be drawn through either side or the back of the unit. It must come from the outdoors (never an attic space or garage), through the closest exterior wall or the floor inside the chase, with water protection as code requires. Outside air requires the fireplace to be secured to the structure so the air duct can't dislodge. Alternatively, the fireplace can draw room air through the space between the surround panels or through air inlet ducts near the floor in the chase. Check local code or CAN/CSA-B365.

The remote heat kit includes a junction box, rheostat and cover plate. For best results, wire its blower to a separate switch or speed controller in the room the outlet is in, on a properly grounded supply.

review.notes: One combined installation & operation manual (100003890, 071124-40) covers both catalog models: the cover and rating label list FP25 LE and FP25AR LE (sold as FP25 Arch LE); the parts list (p. 36) calls it 'FP25 Arch'. All ratings, clearances and install steps are shared; the only per-model numbers are the door, door casting and front trim part numbers (spec card 'Door & trim by model').
